units.title: Unit 21 — In the news
learningObjectives: Recognise natural headline collocations describing political events, electoral outcomes and changes of power.
Use established combinations for police enquiries, public demonstrations, disputes and negotiated settlements.
Distinguish starting talks from reaching agreements and displaying strength from testing strength.
Interpret register differences in journalistic speech reporting and public statements.

items.example: The prime minister decided to call an election after losing parliamentary support.
items.note: Call an election means officially announce that voting will take place; it is not simply request an election.

items.example: The minister agreed to resign from office after the inquiry ended.
items.note: Resign from office is formal language for giving up an official position voluntarily.

items.example: The coalition managed to secure a slim majority in the regional assembly.
items.note: Secure a slim majority means win only a narrow margin of seats or votes.

items.example: The territory voted to declare independence after years of negotiations.
items.note: Declare independence is a formal announcement of political separation.

items.example: Losing every seat in the capital was a humiliating defeat for the party.
items.note: Humiliating intensifies defeat by stressing embarrassment and damaged reputation.

items.example: The cabinet tried to present a show of unity despite disagreements behind closed doors.
items.note: A show of unity is a public display of agreement; private divisions may remain.

items.example: A broad protest movement eventually helped topple a regime that had ruled for decades.
items.note: Topple a regime is frequent in journalism for forcing a government from power.

items.example: The candidate refused to proclaim victory before the final votes were counted.
items.note: Proclaim victory is a formal or journalistic announcement of success.

items.example: Military officers attempted to seize power while the elected leaders were abroad.
items.note: Seize power commonly implies taking control suddenly or by force, not being elected normally.

items.example: The president will deliver a key speech on constitutional reform tomorrow.
items.note: Deliver a speech is formal or journalistic; make or give a speech are also possible.

items.pt: realizar buscas em todo o país
items.example: Investigators had to carry out a nationwide search to locate the missing witness.
items.note: Carry out a search names the organised investigation; nationwide indicates its geographical reach.

items.example: Trouble breaks out whenever the two rival groups confront one another at the station.
items.note: Break out describes the sudden beginning of trouble, violence or unrest.

items.example: Detectives discovered vital clues in photographs taken near the warehouse.
items.note: Vital clues are essential to progress; significant clues may be important but not indispensable.

items.example: Rescue teams will not call off a search while there is a reasonable chance of finding survivors.
items.note: Call off means cancel or stop an ongoing activity, not widen the search.

items.example: The museum offered a substantial reward for information about the stolen sculpture.
items.note: Substantial describes a large amount, unlike a small or token reward.

items.example: The bank hoped the investigation would lead to the recovery of the money.
items.note: Recovery is a natural noun for getting stolen or lost funds back.

items.example: The transport union agreed to enter into talks with city officials on Friday.
items.note: Enter into talks marks the beginning of negotiations, not a completed agreement.

items.example: Both sides hope to reach agreement before the strike deadline.
items.note: Reach agreement means achieve consensus, while enter into talks only starts the process.

items.example: A dispute arises when the partners disagree about how to divide the costs.
items.note: Arise is a common formal verb for the emergence of a problem or disagreement.

items.example: Residents plan to hold demonstrations outside the council offices next week.
items.note: Hold demonstrations describes organising public protests; demonstrations may also be singular.

items.example: The prolonged vote became a test of strength between rival factions.
items.note: A test of strength determines how powerful someone is; a show of strength displays existing power.

items.example: Representatives met overnight to negotiate a settlement to the pay dispute.
items.note: Negotiate a settlement focuses on discussions aimed at ending a disagreement.

items.example: A trusted neighbour agreed to act as a go-between for the two families.
items.note: A go-between conveys messages when parties cannot or will not communicate directly.

items.example: The regional mediator helped broker an agreement on shared water supplies.
items.note: Broker an agreement means facilitate a deal between parties, often through negotiation.

items.example: The council finally chose to bow to public pressure and revise the plan.
items.note: Bow to pressure means yield to demands, usually after initial resistance.

items.example: The universities will enter into an agreement to exchange research staff.
items.note: Enter into an agreement means formally become party to one; it differs from enter into talks.

items.example: The debate will be broadcast on prime-time television to attract a large audience.
items.note: Prime-time describes the period when television typically has its largest audience.

items.example: The spokesperson will hold a press conference once the investigation concludes.
items.note: Hold a press conference is the established combination for an organised meeting with reporters.

items.example: Campaigners warned that the proposal might impose censorship on independent broadcasts.
items.note: Impose censorship means enforce restrictions on what may be published or shown.

items.pt: superar uma ruptura entre pessoas ou grupos
items.example: The joint charity project helped heal a rift between the former allies.
items.note: Heal a rift describes repairing a relationship damaged by serious disagreement.

items.example: Millions of citizens will go to the polls on Sunday to choose a new parliament.
items.note: Go to the polls is a journalistic expression meaning vote in an election.

items.example: The documentary examines how a military coup interrupted the democratic transition.
items.note: A military coup is the seizure of government by armed forces rather than a normal electoral change.

items.example: The large march was designed as a show of strength ahead of the negotiations.
items.note: A show of strength exhibits power; a test of strength explores which side is stronger.

items.example: Forensic experts identified significant clues that narrowed the list of suspects.
items.note: Significant means noteworthy or influential; vital suggests essential to the investigation.

items.example: The student representative will make a speech at the graduation ceremony.
items.note: Make a speech is neutral and everyday; deliver a speech can sound more formal.

items.example: The consultant was asked to broker a deal between the two suppliers.
items.note: Broker naturally combines with deal, agreement and ceasefire in negotiation contexts.

items.example: The association must hold an election whenever the chair steps down.
items.note: Hold an election refers to conducting the voting event; call an election announces it.

items.example: The proposal passed with a narrow majority of just two votes.
items.note: Narrow majority is an alternative to slim majority for a small winning margin.

units.title: Unit 22 — Current affairs
learningObjectives: Use formal press collocations to report official statements, apologies, disclosures and policy disputes.
Recognise established patterns for public disagreement, requests, complaints and reactions.
Distinguish strong refusals, firm public stances and different degrees of disagreement.
Use formal administrative expressions accurately without confusing permission with public reaction.

items.pt: pedir desculpas de maneira profundamente humilde
items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The organisation chose to issue an abject apology after the misconduct was confirmed.
items.note: An abject apology is a strongly humble admission of wrongdoing; the expression is formal.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: Security removed a spectator for disorderly conduct during the concert.
items.note: Disorderly conduct is a relatively formal label for disruptive or unruly behaviour.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The director continued to refuse point-blank to disclose the confidential figures.
items.note: Point-blank after refuse stresses an absolute, unequivocal rejection.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The contractor must provide an explanation for the unexpected delays.
items.note: Provide an explanation is neutral to formal; explain directly is a shorter alternative.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: Further damaging disclosures prompted an independent review of the agency.
items.note: Disclosures reveal private information; damaging stresses harm to reputation or interests.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The watchdog accused the campaign of trying to mislead the electorate about the costs.
items.note: Mislead the electorate means give voters a false or distorted impression.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The minister's public pronouncements were later contradicted by official records.
items.note: Pronouncements sounds more formal and weighty than ordinary comments.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The committee asked the spokesperson to clarify a position that seemed inconsistent.
items.note: Clarify a position means explain an attitude or policy so that it is less ambiguous.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The company chose to decline to comment on the ongoing investigation.
items.note: Decline to comment is a formal, neutral journalistic phrase for refusing to respond.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: New research could reopen a debate about the long-term effects of the policy.
items.note: Reopen a debate means restart discussion of an issue previously considered settled or dormant.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: When evidence emerges of irregular payments, auditors must investigate promptly.
items.note: Emerge is a formal verb for information becoming known or visible.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The association plans to take a firm stance against workplace harassment.
items.note: Take a firm stance signals a clear and determined position, often against something.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The board will flatly reject any proposal that removes basic safeguards.
items.note: Flatly reject means refuse completely and unambiguously, not merely express reservations.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The hospital will issue a statement once the review has finished.
items.note: Issue a statement is a formal collocation for publishing an official message.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The injured climber remained critically ill after emergency surgery.
items.note: Critically ill refers to a life-threatening medical condition, not ordinary illness.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The report said the actor had suffered a massive heart attack while travelling.
items.note: Massive emphasises the severity of the heart attack in nontechnical reporting.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The organisers promised regular updates as the situation developed.
items.note: Regular updates means information supplied repeatedly at reasonably consistent intervals.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: Residents must seek permission before making changes to a listed building.
items.note: Seek permission is formal, especially in administrative or legal settings.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: Witnesses were asked to submit a detailed account of what they observed.
items.note: An account is a report of events; detailed indicates substantial supporting information.

items.section: A · Current affairs in the press
items.example: The applicant was relieved to be given leave to stay after the hearing.
items.note: Leave to stay is a formal immigration-related expression meaning permission to remain.

items.example: Several researchers decided to take issue with the assumptions in the published study.
items.note: Take issue with is formal for openly disagreeing with a claim, view or decision.

items.example: The agency held consultations to gauge public reaction to the proposed route.
items.note: Gauge reaction means assess how people respond, not necessarily persuade them.

items.example: The unexpected resignation may excite speculation about a wider leadership change.
items.note: Excite speculation is relatively formal and means cause rumours or guesses to spread.

items.example: Employees were invited to air grievances at a confidential meeting.
items.note: Air grievances means express complaints openly rather than keep them private.

items.example: A dissenting voice challenged the recommendation during the final vote.
items.note: A dissenting voice denotes someone who disagrees with the majority, often in formal debate.

items.example: She became a vociferous opponent of the proposed mine near the village.
items.note: Vociferous describes loud, outspoken opposition, rather than quiet disagreement.

items.example: The charity director made a passionate entreaty for urgent support.
items.note: An entreaty is an earnest request; passionate shows strong feeling.

items.pt: um comentário casual sem grande intenção
items.example: A throwaway comment in the interview triggered an unexpectedly heated response.
items.note: A throwaway comment is made casually and is not usually intended as a major statement.

items.example: The inspector demanded a satisfactory explanation for the missing documents.
items.note: A satisfactory explanation addresses the concern sufficiently; satisfactory differs from simply detailed.

items.example: Early surveys suggested a divided public reaction to the announcement.
items.note: Public reaction is a common noun phrase for the response of the general population.

items.example: The briefing helped clarify the facts surrounding the funding decision.
items.note: Clarify naturally combines with facts, position and meaning when removing confusion.
